analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 10% surtax on individual incomes above $2 million ($1 million for single filers).
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by five Democratic senators, never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 10% tax on income above $2 million for married couples and $1 million for single filers, on top of existing income taxes. The money would go to the Treasury like any other federal revenue. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the surtax would raise revenue from the roughly 10,000 or so households earning over $2 million. The bill does not earmark that money, so the benefit would come through whatever Congress chose to fund it with, or through lower deficits. No other taxpayer's bill would change.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone except households earning over $2 million

how_it_helps.text: Adds a 10% surtax on the portion of a household's modified adjusted gross income above $2 million, or $1 million for taxpayers not filing jointly.
The surtax applies to all income above the threshold, including investment income, which is currently taxed at lower preferential rates than wages for high earners.
The threshold is not indexed to inflation in the bill text, so over time the surtax would reach more taxpayers as nominal incomes rise.

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income above $2 million per joint return or $1 million for single filers, mostly through wages, business income, and investment gains. Combined with existing rates and the 3.8% net investment income tax, top marginal rates on affected income would exceed 50% in many cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $2 million a year

drawbacks.text: The bill raises revenue but does not direct it to any specific purpose, so its practical benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on what future Congresses do with the money.

The 10% surtax stacks on top of the existing top rate and the 3.8% net investment income tax, pushing combined marginal rates above 50% for affected income, which critics of high top rates argue discourages investment and encourages income shifting.
Because the surtax applies to adjusted gross income with few deductions allowed, filers with volatile income, such as a one-time business sale, could be hit hard in a single year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The surtax targets a very small group of very high earners, so the direct cost to most Americans is zero and the revenue is meaningful. Its weakness is design rather than aim: it dedicates the money to nothing and lacks income smoothing for one-time windfalls. Whether it helps working people in practice depends on how the revenue is used.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Finance Committee, which never scheduled it for a hearing or a vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Van Hollen introduced the Millionaires Surtax Act in the Senate on November 7, 2019, joined by Sen. Sherrod Brown.
The bill imposes a 10% tax on modified adjusted gross income above $2 million, or $1 million for taxpayers not filing jointly.
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.
The bill received no further action of any kind before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $2 million kept the current tax structure and the lower rates on investment income; the bill's sponsors and the general public gained nothing from its death.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The surtax directly takes 10% of income above the threshold, applying to investment income as well as wages. Avoiding it was the concentrated interest at stake in the bill's fate.

A higher top rate on capital gains and business income would give high-income clients more reason to buy tax-planning and deferral strategies. The effect is indirect and the bill never came close to enactment.
